title: The afternoon pause (Berakhot 6b)
hook: a few minutes in the working day; the Talmud says to be especially careful with this prayer
carry: pray in the middle of the day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ein Keloheinu, the song that hides amen in its first letters. Your line was none like him. What one-of-a-kind thing did you notice? Today we leave the morning behind. Day six hundred eight.

Three-fifteen on a weekday. The inbox is full. A meeting just ran long, the kids need picking up, the coffee's gone cold. Nobody plans anything holy for three-fifteen. Morning has its own mood, fresh and new. Night has its own mood, quiet and closing. But the middle of the afternoon is pure busyness. And that's exactly where Jewish tradition puts one of its three daily prayers. In office buildings in some cities, you can find a small group gathering in a conference room for ten minutes, then going back to their desks.
screen: `THREE-FIFTEEN ON A WEEKDAY.` → `NOBODY PLANS ANYTHING HOLY.` → `TEN MINUTES IN A CONFERENCE ROOM.`

segments.voice: The afternoon prayer is called Mincha. The word means a gift, or an offering. The Bible uses it for the Temple's afternoon offering, and the prayer took its name from that hour of the day. It's short: a psalm, the Amidah said silently, and on most weekdays a few closing lines. A matter of minutes. The Talmud links each daily prayer to one of the ancestors, and gives the afternoon to Isaac. In Genesis, in the old Jewish translation, "Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." The rabbis read that meditation as prayer. Isaac, alone in a field toward evening, before he even sees Rebekah coming. Now the line from the Talmud this day is named for. In tractate Berakhot, page 6b, a teacher says in the name of another: a person should always be especially careful with the afternoon prayer. Why this one? Later commentators give a plain answer. Morning prayer comes before the day starts, and evening prayer comes after it ends. But Mincha lands right in the middle, when you're busiest and it's easiest to let it slip. Being careful with it means stepping out of the stream on purpose. The Talmud gives its own reason too, a story about a prophet on a mountain, and that's tomorrow. Today, just the shape of it: a gift given in the middle of the day.
screen: `MINCHA: A GIFT, AN OFFERING.` · `ISAAC IN THE FIELD AT EVENTIDE.` · `BE ESPECIALLY CAREFUL WITH IT.` · `THE BUSIEST HOUR.` · then, large: `PRAY IN THE MIDDLE OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause mid-afternoon. If it's afternoon now, good. If not, practice it here, and set a reminder for later. Stop what you're doing. Stand or sit up straight. Close your eyes. Breathe out the last hour. If you pray, this is a moment for it, in any words you have. If you don't, just stand in the middle of your day like Isaac in his field, and look around. The bell holds the time.
Mincha. A gift, an offering. The short afternoon prayer, said in the busiest part of the day.
Your line: pray in the middle of the day. Set one alarm for mid-afternoon today, and when it rings, stop for one full minute. Day six hundred eight.

howItsDone: Mincha is said daily from early afternoon until sunset: Ashrei (Psalm 145), the silent Amidah with its repetition when there is a minyan, and on most weekdays Tachanun and Aleinu. Many people gather for it at work or between errands.

fork.setup: it's three-fifteen. your day is packed. the Talmud says to be especially careful with which prayer?
fork.reveal: Berakhot 6b: always be careful with Mincha, the one that falls in the middle of the busy day.

original.note: Hebrew: a gift or offering. the name of the afternoon prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: the afternoon one of three prayers.
what it means: a short gift carved out of the busiest hour of the day.
what a scholar hears: named for the afternoon offering, linked to Isaac in Berakhot 26b, singled out for care in Berakhot 6b.

notes: Genesis 24:63 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Berakhot 6b: Rabbi Helbo in the name of Rav Huna; the Elijah reason is held for day 609.
The 'middle of the busy day' explanation is from later commentators (e.g., the Tur, Orach Chayim 232); confirm attribution.
Mincha name: from the afternoon offering (minchat ha'erev / the afternoon tamid); simplified as 'a meal offering in the afternoon'; Keeper may prefer 'the afternoon offering'.

Editor review (y2 595–612): 'a meal offering was brought in the afternoon' was misleading (the afternoon tamid was an animal offering; the hour is called the time of the mincha, e.g. 1 Kings 18:36, Psalm 141:2), so it now says the Bible uses the word for the Temple's afternoon offering. Unsourced 'ten or fifteen minutes' removed from teach and myth. The 1 Kings 18:36 verse itself is left for day 609.
